text: The Puerto Rico Status Act, H.R. 2757, was a bill introduced during the 116th United States Congress with the goal of granting Puerto Rico, an unincorporated U.S. territory, admission into the Union as a state. The bill was originally introduced in the 116th Congress and was reintroduced as H.R. 1522 on March 2, 2021, in the 117th Congress. It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources, with the last action taken on June 16, 2021. In 1898, after the Spanish–American War, Spain ceded Puerto Rico and its surrounding archipelago to the United States. From 1900 onward, measures were enacted to establish local civilian government, beginning with the creation of the elected House of Delegates in 1900 and the establishment of the Resident Commissioner position in 1902. The Resident Commissioner was a non-voting member of the U.S. House of Representatives, intended to represent Puerto Rico’s interests in Congress, though the title was not used as "delegate" to avoid implying a path toward statehood, given that territories acquired through war were not guaranteed such status. In 1917, the Jones–Shafroth Act created an elected Senate and granted U.S. citizenship to all Puerto Ricans born after April 25, 1898. In 1947, the Elective Governor Act granted Puerto Rico its first elected governor, and in 1950, the territory was granted the right to hold a constitutional convention. The resulting constitution, approved in a 1952 referendum, changed Puerto Rico’s status to an unincorporated "Commonwealth," a territory under federal control but not fully bound by the U.S. Constitution. Puerto Rico is the largest U.S. overseas territory by both size and population, with a population of about 3 million. Its current political status denies Puerto Ricans the right to vote for the U.S. president or have full representation in Congress. Statehood would grant Puerto Rico two U.S. Senators and a number of House Representatives; the Huntington–Hill method estimates four House seats. It would also provide Puerto Rico with electoral votes in the presidential election and greater access to federal funding, an issue highlighted by the damage from Hurricane Maria in 2017, which caused up to $90 billion in damage and drew criticism of the federal response. In 2017, following the pro-statehood Partido Nuevo Progresista (PNP) gaining control of the Legislative Assembly and the governorship, Puerto Rico appointed a delegation of shadow congresspeople—two senators and five representatives—by the Puerto Rico Equality Commission to lobby Congress on statehood. Multiple referendums have been held on Puerto Rico’s future status, beginning in 1967, with support for statehood steadily increasing despite changes in referendum design. The most recent prior to 2019 was in 2017, where 97% of voters chose statehood, though turnout was just over 22% due to a boycott by major political parties. In 2017, Jenniffer González Colón, the non-voting Resident Commissioner, introduced a bill requiring Congress to support a status vote and, if statehood was chosen, to prepare for admission by January 3, 2025, including amending or repealing relevant territorial laws. The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources but did not reach a vote. In October 2019, José E. Serrano, a Democratic congressman from New York and a native of Puerto Rico, introduced a new bill with 60 cosponsors—42 Democrats and 18 Republicans—to achieve Puerto Rico’s admission, which was also referred to the Committee on Natural Resources and did not reach a vote in the full House. A corresponding bill, the Law for the Final Definition of the Political Status of Puerto Rico, was introduced in Puerto Rico’s Legislative Assembly and approved by both chambers in March 2020, leading to the 2020 plebiscite, which resulted in a majority in favor of statehood. Although the 2020 plebiscite showed a majority for statehood, turnout was just over 52%, with 623,000 of the 2.3 million registered voters supporting statehood. While U.S. opinion polls have consistently favored Puerto Rico’s admission since the 1960s, there is a higher degree of ambivalence in Puerto Rico due to concerns about national identity, as illustrated by the fact that the pro-independence Partido Independentista Puertorriqueño (PIP) candidate received 14% of the vote in the 2020 gubernatorial election. Although both major U.S. parties have included statehood in their platforms, senior Republican figures, including Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell in 2019, opposed Puerto Rico’s admission, calling it "full-bore socialism" and warning it would increase Democratic representation in the Senate. Despite this, at the time of the 2020 vote, the Governor, Resident Commissioner, Speaker of the Puerto Rico House of Representatives, and President of the Puerto Rico Senate—all members of the pro-statehood PNP—were also conservative Republicans. Following the 2020 vote, legislators of both parties expressed willingness to open a debate on Puerto Rico’s status in Congress. As of January 3, 2025, the deadline for Puerto Rico’s potential admission under the 2017 bill remains unmet.
